01 What is Rhinoceros 3D?

Overview

Rhinoceros 3D (Rhino) is a professional 3D modelling application used across architecture, product design, jewellery, marine engineering and industrial design. It is built on NURBS geometry — a mathematically precise way of representing curves and surfaces that allows for extremely accurate models.

Unlike mesh-based tools such as Blender or SketchUp, Rhino works with smooth, editable mathematical curves that can be scaled to any size without losing quality — ideal for manufactured objects and technical drawings.

Who Uses Rhino?

IndustryCommon Uses
ArchitectureBuilding facades, complex geometry, BIM workflows
Product DesignConsumer goods, prototypes, CAD for manufacturing
JewelleryRings, pendants, organic forms, casting preparation
Marine / AerospaceHull design, fuselage surfaces, precision parts
FashionShoe design, accessories, pattern making

What is NURBS?

NURBS stands for Non-Uniform Rational B-Spline. Practically, this means:

  • Curves are defined by control points, not pixels or polygons
  • You can scale a model from 1mm to 100m with no loss of precision
  • Surfaces are created from curves — good curves lead to good surfaces
💡 Key Insight:Everything in Rhino starts with a curve. Mastering 2D curves is the single most important skill you can build as a beginner.
✏ TRY IT  —  Explore Rhino's Launch Screen
  1. 1Open Rhinoceros 8. On the splash screen choose Small Objects — Millimeters as your template.
  2. 2Hover over each viewport label (Top, Front, Right, Perspective) and read their names.
  3. 3Click the Perspective viewport, hold Right-click and drag — notice the 3D rotation.
  4. 4Click the Top viewport and try the same drag — notice it does NOT rotate (2D viewports are locked flat).
  5. 5Type Help in the command line and press Enter. Browse the Help panel — your reference library.
02 The Rhino 8 Interface

First Launch

When Rhino opens you will see a large workspace divided into four panels. Each part has a clear purpose. Within a few sessions it will feel completely natural.

Fig 1. The Rhinoceros 8 workspace — full interface overview

The Four Viewports

ViewportWhat It Shows
TopLooking straight down the Z-axis. Your main 2D drawing area.
FrontLooking along the Y-axis — shows width and height (X and Z).
RightLooking along the X-axis — shows depth and height (Y and Z).
PerspectiveA 3D camera view. Rotate freely to inspect your model.
Fig 2. The four viewports — Top, Perspective, Front and Right
💡 Pro Tip:Double-click any viewport title to maximise it to full screen. Double-click again to return to 4-panel view.

The Interface at a Glance

Fig 3. The Rhino 8 menu bar, Command line and toolbar ribbon
AreaLocation & Purpose
Menu BarTop of screen. File, Edit, Curve, Surface menus — browse to discover commands.
Command LineBelow the menu. THE most important area. Always read its prompts.
ToolbarsLeft side and top. Icon shortcuts for common commands.
ViewportsThe large central area. Four views of your workspace.

OSnap PanelLeft sidebar in Rhino 8. Controls snapping (End, Mid, Cen etc.).

Fig 4. Left sidebar toolbar
⚠️ Important:Always watch the Command Line. Rhino tells you what it expects next — it will say things like "Pick first point" or "Radius <1.0>". If confused, look there first.
✏ TRY IT  —  Map the Interface
  1. 1Locate every area in the table above — Menu Bar, Command Line, Toolbars, Properties Panel, OSnap Panel, Status Bar.
  2. 2Open the Curve menu. Browse the options without clicking — notice how commands are organised by type.
  3. 3Open View → Zoom and look at the submenu. Close when done.
  4. 4Double-click the Perspective viewport title to maximise it, then double-click again to return to four viewports.
  5. 5Hover over 5 different toolbar icons on the left sidebar and read each tooltip that appears.
03 Navigating Your Workspace

Mouse Controls

Fig 5. Top and Perspective viewports — double-click any title to expand
ActionHow To Do It
Rotate (3D)Right-click + drag (Perspective viewport only)
PanShift + Right-click + drag (all viewports)
ZoomScroll wheel
Zoom preciseCtrl + Right-click + drag
Zoom ExtentsZ then E — frames everything instantly
Zoom to WindowZ then W — drag a box to zoom
💡 Habit:Press Z then E constantly. Whenever something disappears or you get lost, this brings everything back.

Keyboard Shortcuts

ShortcutAction
Z then EZoom Extents — see everything
Z then AZoom All Extents — fit all four viewports
Ctrl + ZUndo
EscapeCancel any active command
F10Toggle control points on selected curve
F11Hide all control points

The Construction Plane (CPlane)

Each viewport has an invisible flat surface. When you click to place points, Rhino places them on this plane.

  • Top viewport = flat X/Y — perfect for 2D drawing
  • Front viewport = vertical X/Z wall
  • Right viewport = vertical Y/Z wall
💡 Key Rule:Always check which viewport has the yellow border (active). The active viewport determines which CPlane your geometry lands on.
✏ TRY IT  —  Master Navigation Controls
  1. 1In Perspective, hold Right-click and drag in all directions. Orbit slowly around the grid center.
  2. 2Hold Shift + Right-click and drag — notice it pans instead of rotating.
  3. 3Scroll to zoom very close to the grid, then press Z then E to instantly zoom back out.
  4. 4Double-click the Top viewport to maximise. Press Z then A to fit all four viewports at once.
  5. 5Click in the Front viewport and move your cursor — watch the Y coordinate in the status bar stay at 0 (flat CPlane).
04 Precision Tools

Object Snaps (OSnap)

Object Snaps magnetically pull your cursor to specific geometric points — making perfectly accurate drawing possible.

Fig 6. The OSnap panel — enable these for precise drafting
SnapSnaps To...
EndThe endpoint of a line, curve or edge
MidThe midpoint of any curve or line
CenThe centre of a circle or arc
IntWhere two curves cross each other
NearThe closest point on any curve
PointAny standalone point object
💡 Visual Cue:When a snap activates, a small coloured marker appears on screen. Watch for it before clicking — it confirms your precision.

The Gumball

The Gumball is a 3D manipulator that appears on selected objects. Coloured arrows and arcs let you move, rotate and scale without typing a command.

  • Red arrow = move along X-axis
  • Green arrow = move along Y-axis
  • Blue arrow = move along Z-axis
  • Coloured arcs = rotate around that axis
💡 Toggle:Press the Gumball button in the status bar or type Gumball in the command line.
✏ TRY IT  —  Practice OSnaps & the Gumball
  1. 1Check the OSnap panel — make sure End, Mid, Cen and Int are ticked on.
  2. 2Draw a Rectangle. Type Line — hover over a corner until the End snap marker appears, then click precisely.
  3. 3Hover over the midpoint of one side — the Mid snap appears. Click to start a line exactly there.
  4. 4Select the rectangle. Drag the red Gumball arrow to slide it along X only. Press Ctrl+Z to undo.
  5. 5Type Circle, click inside the rectangle — watch the Cen snap appear near the middle.
05 The Command Line

How It Works

The Command Line is Rhino's control centre. Almost every action can be typed here, and Rhino constantly updates it with instructions as you work.

  • Prompts — tell you what to do next, e.g. "Start of line"
  • Option toggles — clickable options appear in brackets, e.g. Cap=Yes
  • Default values — shown as <1.0> — press Enter to accept
💡 Auto-complete:As you type, Rhino suggests completions. Press Tab or Enter to accept. This dramatically speeds up your workflow.
⚠️ Common Mistake:If typing does nothing, press Escape once to clear any active command, then start typing again.
✏ TRY IT  —  Get Comfortable with the Command Line
  1. 1Type Ci — watch autocomplete suggestions appear. Press Escape to cancel.
  2. 2Type Circle and press Enter. Read the prompt: "Center of circle". Click a point.
  3. 3The prompt says "Radius". Type 50 and press Enter — a perfect 50-unit circle appears.
  4. 4Type Circle again. After clicking the centre, click Diameter in the command options. Type 100 and Enter.
  5. 5Type Undo and press Enter twice to remove both circles.
06 Introduction to 2D Curves

What Are Curves in Rhino?

Curves are the building blocks of everything you create — from a simple straight line to a complex freeform shape. Every curve has two key properties:

  • Open or Closed: An open curve has two endpoints. A closed curve forms a complete loop.
  • Degree: The mathematical complexity. Degree 1 = straight lines. Degree 3 = smooth curves.
💡 Why It Matters:When you later extrude curves into 3D, Rhino requires closed curves to make solid objects. Open curves create open surfaces.

Core Curve Commands

Work through each green exercise below in order — all in the Top viewport. Click any command header to expand its exercise.

Fig 7. The Lines floating toolbar — quick access to Line, Polyline and related tools
CommandWhat It Creates
LineA straight line between two clicked points
PolylineMultiple connected straight segments
RectangleA four-sided closed shape
CircleA circle — centre point plus radius
ArcPart of a circle
EllipseAn oval shape
CurveA smooth freeform NURBS curve
InterpCrvInterpolated curve — passes exactly through every point clicked
╱ Line Draw a precise straight line between two points ▾
  1. 1Make the Top viewport active (click in it — its border turns yellow).
  2. 2Click the Line icon in the left toolbar, or type Line and press Enter.
  3. 3The command line says "Start of line". Click anywhere on the grid.
  4. 4Instead of clicking the end, type 150 and press Enter — a line exactly 150 units long appears in the direction you were pointing.
  5. 5Select the line and check its length in the Properties panel on the right.
💡 Tip: Hold Shift while dragging to constrain to exact 0°, 45°, or 90° angles.
⌒ Polyline Trace a multi-segment path by clicking multiple points ▾
  1. 1Type Polyline and press Enter.
  2. 2Click five or six points forming a rough Z or W shape across the viewport.
  3. 3To close the polyline into a loop, type C and press Enter on your last segment.
  4. 4Press Escape if you want to leave it open instead. Compare the two results.
  5. 5Press F10 to see the individual corner control points appear as yellow dots.
💡 Tip: Polyline is great for tracing over imported images or sketches — each click defines an exact corner.
▭ Rectangle Draw a precise four-sided closed shape ▾
  1. 1Type Rectangle and press Enter. Click a corner point on the grid.
  2. 2Instead of clicking the second corner, type 200,100 and press Enter — a rectangle exactly 200 × 100 units appears.
  3. 3Draw a second rectangle. In the command options click 3Point — this lets you draw a rotated rectangle.
  4. 4Select your first rectangle and press F10 — notice it has exactly 4 corner control points.
  5. 5Type Area, select the rectangle, press Enter — Rhino reports its exact area in the command line.
💡 Tip: Typing exact X,Y coordinates after the first point is the fastest way to draw precise rectangles every time.
○ Circle Draw perfect circles by centre, diameter or through points ▾
  1. 1Type Circle and press Enter. Click a centre point, then type 60 and Enter — radius 60.
  2. 2Type Circle again. After clicking the centre, click Diameter in the options, type 100 — diameter 100 (radius 50).
  3. 3Type Circle once more. In the options click 3Point. Click three points anywhere — Rhino draws the unique circle through all three.
  4. 4Draw a rectangle first, then draw a circle — use the OSnap Cen snap to find the exact centre of the rectangle.
  5. 5Select any circle and press F10 — notice its single centre control point and the four quadrant points.
💡 Tip: The circle command is the gateway to cylinders, holes, and arcs in 3D. Master it early.
◜ Arc Draw a curved arc — a portion of a circle ▾
  1. 1Type Arc and press Enter. Click a centre, then a start point. Drag your cursor — watch the arc sweep. Click to finish.
  2. 2Type Arc again. In the options click 3Point. Click three points — the arc passes through all three exactly.
  3. 3Draw a straight line first. Type Arc, use Tangent mode — click the line's endpoint as the start. The arc departs tangentially from the line.
  4. 4Draw a door opening: draw a rectangle, type Explode, delete one short wall, then draw a 90° arc from the gap curving into the room.
  5. 5Select your arc and press F10 — notice the start, end and centre control points.
💡 Tip: Arcs are essential for doors, rounded transitions, and any partial-circle geometry in plans or profiles.
⬭ Ellipse Draw oval shapes with two different radii ▾
  1. 1Type Ellipse and press Enter. Click a centre point.
  2. 2The prompt says "End of first axis". Move right and type 80 — X-radius = 80.
  3. 3The prompt says "End of second axis". Move up and type 40 — Y-radius = 40. A wide flat ellipse appears.
  4. 4Type Ellipse again. In the options choose FromFoci — click two focus points, then drag to set the width.
  5. 5Draw a circle and an ellipse of similar size. Press F10 on each and compare their control point structures.
💡 Tip: Ellipses are useful for organic plan shapes, eyes, eggs, vehicle cross-sections and many natural forms.
〜 Curve Draw smooth freeform NURBS curves through control points ▾
  1. 1Type Curve and press Enter. Click 6–8 points in a flowing S-wave across the viewport.
  2. 2Press Enter to finish. Notice the curve is smooth — it flows near your points but may not pass exactly through all of them.
  3. 3Press F10. Drag several yellow control points to reshape the curve. Press F11 when done.
  4. 4Type Curve again. Place points in a circular pattern, then type C and Enter to close it smoothly.
  5. 5Compare with a Rectangle — the closed Curve has smooth rounded corners, while Rectangle has sharp 90° corners.
💡 Tip: Degree 3 (the default) gives the smoothest results. Use Curve for organic, flowing shapes where exact point location matters less.
∿ InterpCrv Draw a smooth curve that passes exactly through every clicked point ▾
  1. 1Type InterpCrv and press Enter. Click 5–6 points forming a gentle wave.
  2. 2Press Enter to finish. Notice the curve passes exactly through every point you clicked — different from the Curve command.
  3. 3Press F10 and compare the number and position of control points vs. a Curve command result.
  4. 4Type InterpCrv, place points in a teardrop shape, then type C and Enter to close it. Good for leaf or petal profiles.
  5. 5Select the InterpCrv and use the Gumball to scale it — hold Shift while dragging a scale handle for uniform scaling.
💡 Tip: Use InterpCrv when the curve must hit specific measured locations — e.g. profiling a chair leg or an arch that must pass through set heights.
✏ TRY IT  —  Identify Open and Closed Curves
  1. 1Draw one of each: Line, Circle, Rectangle and a Curve.
  2. 2Select the Line — check the Properties panel. It should say "Open".
  3. 3Select the Circle — it should say "Closed".
  4. 4Draw a Polyline with 4 points but do NOT close it. Draw another and type C to close it. Compare them.
  5. 5Select all objects with Ctrl+A. Check how many are shown in the status bar.
07 Editing & Modifying Curves

Selecting Objects

MethodHow It Works
ClickClick directly on a curve to select it
Window SelectDrag left→right — selects fully enclosed objects
Crossing SelectDrag right→left — selects anything the box touches
Select AllCtrl + A
DeselectEscape or click empty space

Essential Editing Commands

CommandWhat It Does
MoveMoves selected objects. Click start point then end point.
CopyCopies objects. Same as Move but originals remain.
RotateRotates objects. Click centre, then start and end angles.
ScaleResizes objects. Click base point, type scale factor.
MirrorCreates mirrored copy. Draw the mirror axis line.
TrimCuts one curve where it intersects another.
ExtendLengthens a curve to meet another curve.
FilletRounds a corner between two curves.
ChamferCuts a corner diagonally.
JoinConnects curves sharing endpoints into one polycurve.
ExplodeBreaks a joined curve into individual segments.
OffsetCreates a parallel copy at a specified distance.
⚠️ Trim Tip:First select the cutting object, press Enter, then click the part to remove. Beginners often get this backwards.
💡 Fillet vs Chamfer:Use Fillet for rounded corners (smooth arcs). Use Chamfer for diagonal cuts. Both require two intersecting or near-intersecting curves.
✏ TRY IT  —  Edit, Trim & Transform Curves
  1. 1Draw two overlapping circles. Type Trim, click one circle as cutter, Enter, then click the overlapping segment of the second.
  2. 2Draw a Rectangle. Type Explode to break it into 4 lines. Type Fillet, radius 20, click two adjacent sides near a corner.
  3. 3Draw a circle. Type Offset, type 20, click the circle and outside it for a larger copy. Try inside for a smaller one.
  4. 4Draw a line. Type Copy, select it, Enter, click a base, place 3 copies in a row, press Enter.
  5. 5Select all with Ctrl+A. Type Mirror, click two points for a vertical axis. All objects mirror across.
08 Practice Project: Floor Plan

Draw a Room Floor Plan

This exercise combines everything — Rectangle, Circle, Arc, Trim, Fillet, Offset and OSnap — into a single practical task. Draw a rectangular room 600 × 400 units with a door opening, circular table and window recess.

✏ FLOOR PLAN — Step by Step
  1. 1Type Rectangle. Click a corner, type 600,400 and Enter.
  2. 2Type Explode — select the rectangle, press Enter. Now you have 4 individual wall lines.
  3. 3Door gap: use Line to mark 90-unit sections on the bottom wall, then delete the middle segment.
  4. 4Door swing: type Arc and draw a 90° arc from the gap, curving into the room.
  5. 5Table: type Circle, click the room centre, type 60 for radius.
  6. 6Window: type Offset on the top wall, offset inward 15 units. Trim and Fillet the corners.
  7. 7Press Z then E to see your finished plan. Does it have a door, table and window?
💡 Checkpoint:If your plan looks like a room with a door swing, circular table and window recess — you have used every core 2D skill in this guide. Well done!

10 Layers & Organisation

What Are Layers?

Layers are how Rhino organises geometry into named, colour-coded groups. Think of them like transparent sheets stacked on top of each other — each sheet holds specific objects, and you can show, hide, lock or colour each one independently.

Using layers keeps your model clean and manageable. A floor plan might have separate layers for Walls, Furniture, Dimensions and Annotations — so you can turn each group on or off without affecting the others.

Fig 8. The Layers panel in Rhino 8 — Default layer plus five named layers with colour assignments

The Layers Panel — What Each Column Means

ColumnWhat It Controls
Layer nameThe name you give the layer — double-click to rename
Visibility (eye icon)Click to show or hide all objects on that layer
Lock (padlock icon)Locked layers are visible but cannot be selected or edited
Colour swatchThe display colour for all objects on that layer
MaterialRender material assigned to the layer
LinetypeLine style (continuous, dashed etc.) for 2D drawing output
Print WidthLine weight when printing or exporting to PDF

Opening the Layers Panel

If the Layers panel is not visible, open it by going to Panels → Layers in the menu, or type Layer in the command line and press Enter.

💡 Shortcut:The Layers panel is usually docked on the right side of the screen. If you accidentally close it, just go to Panels → Layers to bring it back.

Creating and Naming Layers

Good layer naming is a professional habit worth building from day one. Use clear, descriptive names that describe what the layer contains.

ActionHow To Do It
Create new layerClick the + button at the top of the Layers panel, or type Layer → New
Rename a layerDouble-click the layer name and type the new name
Delete a layerSelect it and click the × button (only works if the layer is empty)
Set active layerClick the layer name once — the tick mark moves to show the current layer
Change layer colourClick the colour swatch to open the colour picker
Hide/show layerClick the lightbulb icon to toggle visibility
Lock a layerClick the padlock icon — objects are visible but protected

Assigning Layer Colours

Fig 9. The Rhino colour picker — HSV wheel with hex input for precise colours

Clicking a layer's colour swatch opens the full colour picker. You can choose from the preset list on the left, use the HSV colour wheel, or type a hex code directly. Each layer should have a distinct colour so you can instantly identify which layer geometry belongs to when working.

💡 Good Layer Colours:Use high-contrast colours between layers — avoid colours that look similar. A common convention: red for walls, blue for annotations, green for furniture, yellow for dimensions, white or grey for construction lines.

Geometry on Different Layers

Fig 10. Three layers in use — green circle, red polyline and black curves each on their own layer

In the screenshot above you can clearly see three layers of geometry displayed simultaneously. Each object's colour tells you immediately which layer it belongs to. This makes complex models much easier to navigate and edit.

Moving Objects Between Layers

You will often draw something on the wrong layer and need to reassign it. There are two ways:

MethodSteps
Properties panelSelect the object → in the Properties panel on the right, click the Layer dropdown and choose the target layer
Drag in Layers panelSelect object(s) → right-click in the Layers panel → Change Object Layer → pick the layer
ChangeLayer commandSelect objects, type ChangeLayer, press Enter, choose the target layer
⚠️ Common Mistake:Drawing on the wrong layer is extremely common. Always check which layer is active (has the tick mark) before you start drawing. Make it a habit to set your layer first, then draw.

Recommended Layer Structure for Beginners

For a basic architectural or product drawing, start with this layer setup:

Layer NameColourContains
00_ConstructionGreyReference lines, grids, temporary geometry
01_CurvesWhiteAll 2D working curves
02_SurfacesCyanOpen 3D surfaces
03_SolidsBlueClosed 3D polysurfaces and solids
04_AnnotationsYellowDimensions, text, leaders
✏ TRY IT  —  Set Up and Use Layers
  1. 1Open the Layers panel (Panels → Layers). Click + three times to create three new layers.
  2. 2Double-click each layer name and rename them: Curves, Circles, Construction.
  3. 3Click the colour swatch on Curves and set it to Red. Set Circles to Green. Set Construction to Grey.
  4. 4Click the Curves layer to make it active (tick appears). Draw a Rectangle and a Polyline. They should appear red.
  5. 5Click the Circles layer to make it active. Draw two circles. They should appear green.
  6. 6Click the lightbulb next to Circles to hide it — your circles disappear. Click again to show them.
  7. 7Select one red curve. In the Properties panel, change its layer to Circles — it turns green instantly.
11 Extrude to 3D

From 2D Curves to 3D Objects

Extruding is the most fundamental way to create 3D geometry in Rhino. It takes a 2D curve and pushes it through space to create a surface or solid. A circle becomes a cylinder. A rectangle becomes a box. Any closed curve becomes a solid shape.

This is the bridge between the 2D drafting skills you have built and full 3D modelling. Master this one command and you can build an enormous range of objects.

Fig 11. A circle in the Top viewport extruded into a solid cylinder — visible in all four viewports

The Solid Tools Toolbar

Fig 12. The Solid Tools toolbar — extrude and boolean operations

The Solid Tools toolbar (shown above) contains the main extrude commands alongside boolean and solid editing tools. You can access these by clicking their icons, or by typing the command name directly.

Open vs Closed Curves — Critical Difference

Curve TypeWhat Extrude Produces
Closed curve (circle, rectangle, closed polyline)A solid with flat caps on both ends — a true solid object
Open curve (line, arc, open polyline)An open surface — a sheet with no caps, not a solid
💡 Key Rule:Always use closed curves when you want a solid 3D object. If your extrude produces an open surface instead of a solid, check that your input curve is properly closed — select it and check the Properties panel.

ExtrudeCrv — The Main Command

ExtrudeCrv is the workhorse extrude command. It pushes any curve a specified distance along the Z-axis (or any direction you choose).

StepWhat to Do
1. Draw a closed curveDraw a Rectangle or Circle in the Top viewport
2. Type ExtrudeCrvPress Enter — or click the Extrude icon in Solid Tools
3. Select the curveClick your closed curve, press Enter
4. Set the distanceType a value (e.g. 100) and press Enter — or click and drag in the Front viewport
5. Check the resultSwitch to Perspective viewport to see your 3D solid

Important ExtrudeCrv Options

When you run ExtrudeCrv, the command line shows several options. These are the most important ones:

OptionWhat It Does
Cap=YesCloses the ends of the extrusion — creates a solid. Keep this on for most work.
Cap=NoLeaves the ends open — creates an open surface (a tube or shell).
BothSidesExtrudes equally in both directions from the curve plane.
DirectionLets you pick a custom extrude direction instead of straight up the Z-axis.
TwoPointsDefine the extrude path by clicking two points in any viewport.
⚠️ Cap=Yes:Always check that Cap=Yes is set in the command options before pressing Enter. If it says Cap=No, click it to toggle. Without caps, your extrusion will be hollow — an open surface rather than a solid.

Viewing Your 3D Model

Once you have a 3D solid, the Perspective viewport is your main view. Use these display modes to see it clearly:

Display ModeHow to SwitchBest For
WireframeRight-click viewport title → WireframeSeeing all edges and curves clearly
ShadedRight-click viewport title → ShadedSeeing the solid form and volume
RenderedRight-click viewport title → RenderedPreview with materials and lighting
GhostedRight-click viewport title → GhostedSee through the solid to inner geometry

Other Extrude Commands

CommandWhat It Does
ExtrudeCrvStandard straight extrusion — most used
ExtrudeCrvTaperedExtrudes with a draft angle — walls taper inward or outward
ExtrudeCrvAlongCrvPushes a profile curve along a path curve — for sweeping shapes
ExtrudeSrfExtrudes a surface face rather than a curve
ExtrudePointExtrudes a curve to a single point — creates a cone or pyramid shape
⬆ ExtrudeCrv Push a 2D closed curve into a 3D solid ▾
  1. 1In the Top viewport, draw a Circle with radius 50. Make sure it is a closed curve.
  2. 2Type ExtrudeCrv and press Enter. Click the circle to select it, then press Enter.
  3. 3Check the command line — make sure it says Cap=Yes. If it says Cap=No, click it to toggle.
  4. 4Type 100 and press Enter. Switch to the Perspective viewport — you have a solid cylinder 100 units tall.
  5. 5Right-click the Perspective viewport title and choose Shaded. Your cylinder now shows as a solid green form.
💡 Tip: Try extruding a Rectangle (box), a closed Polyline (prism) and an Ellipse (oval column) — each closed curve produces a different solid shape.
△ ExtrudeCrvTapered Extrude with walls that angle inward or outward ▾
  1. 1Draw a Rectangle in the Top viewport.
  2. 2Type ExtrudeCrvTapered and press Enter. Select the rectangle, press Enter.
  3. 3The command asks for a Draft angle. Type 5 and press Enter — this gives 5° of taper.
  4. 4Type 80 for the height and press Enter. View in Perspective — the walls angle inward like a pyramid frustum.
  5. 5Try a negative draft angle (type -5) — the walls flare outward instead.
💡 Tip: Tapered extrusions are used for moulded plastic parts, architectural columns, jewellery bezels, and any shape that must be removed from a mould.
↗ ExtrudeCrvAlongCrv Sweep a profile along a custom path ▾
  1. 1In the Top viewport draw a small Circle (radius 10) — this is your profile.
  2. 2In the Front viewport draw a Curve sweeping upward and to the side — this is your path.
  3. 3Type ExtrudeCrvAlongCrv and press Enter.
  4. 4The command asks for the curve to extrude — click the circle. Press Enter.
  5. 5The command asks for the path curve — click the arc or curve in the Front viewport. Press Enter. A tube follows the path.
💡 Tip: This is ideal for pipes, handrails, cables, tube furniture and any object that follows a curved path through space.
✏ TRY IT  —  Build a Simple 3D Scene
  1. 1Create two layers: Floor (grey) and Columns (blue). Set Floor as active.
  2. 2In the Top viewport, draw a large Rectangle (600 × 400). Type ExtrudeCrv, select it, Cap=Yes, height 10. You have a floor slab.
  3. 3Switch to the Columns layer. Draw four small Circles (radius 15) near the corners of your floor plan.
  4. 4Select all four circles. Type ExtrudeCrv, Cap=Yes, height 200. Four columns rise from the floor.
  5. 5In Perspective, right-click the viewport title and switch to Shaded. Toggle the Columns layer on and off to see the effect.
  6. 6Press Z then E to frame everything. Orbit around your model with Right-click drag.
🔧

Pathway Unlocked — MultiCam CNC Router

With layers and extrude mastered you can now prepare 2D and 3D files for the MultiCam using Fusion 360 CAM. Complete Section 12 (Booleans) first for the full 3D workflow. See Section 14 for the full pathway.

12 Boolean Operations

What Are Boolean Operations?

Boolean operations are how you combine, subtract and intersect 3D solids to create complex shapes. Named after mathematician George Boole, they are the primary modelling tool for mechanical parts, product design and architectural components.

Think of them like logical operations on physical objects — you can add two shapes together, cut one out of another, or keep only the part where they overlap. All three operations require closed polysurfaces (solids) — open surfaces will not work.

💡 Before You Start:Always check your objects are closed solids before running a Boolean. Select an object and look at the Properties panel — it should say "Closed polysurface". If it says "Open polysurface", you have naked edges to fix first.

The Three Boolean Commands

CommandWhat It DoesResult
BooleanUnionMerges two or more solids into one single solidOne combined closed solid — internal walls removed
BooleanDifferenceSubtracts one solid from another — cuts a hole or removes materialFirst solid with the second solid's shape removed
BooleanIntersectionKeeps only the volume where both solids overlapOnly the intersecting region — everything else deleted
Fig 13. Before any Boolean — a cylinder and tapered pentagon base sitting as two separate solids

BooleanUnion — Merging Solids

BooleanUnion combines two or more overlapping solids into a single seamless solid. The internal shared walls are automatically removed. Use this to build up complex shapes from simple primitives.

∪ BooleanUnion Merge two overlapping solids into one ▾
  1. 1Draw a Rectangle (200 × 100) in the Top viewport. Extrude it 50 units with ExtrudeCrv, Cap=Yes. This is your base box.
  2. 2Draw a Circle (radius 40) overlapping one end of the rectangle. Extrude it 80 units, Cap=Yes. This is your cylinder.
  3. 3Type BooleanUnion and press Enter.
  4. 4Select both solids (click one, then Shift+click the other). Press Enter.
  5. 5Switch to Shaded view in Perspective — the two shapes are now a single merged solid. The internal shared wall is gone.
💡 Tip: You can union more than two objects at once — just select all of them before pressing Enter.
Fig 14. BooleanUnion / Split result — the two solids combined showing merged geometry

BooleanDifference — Cutting Holes

BooleanDifference subtracts one solid from another. The first object you select is what you are cutting from. The second is the cutting tool. This is how you create holes, pockets, slots and recesses.

∖ BooleanDifference Cut one solid out of another ▾
  1. 1Create a box: draw a Rectangle (200 × 150) and extrude 60 units, Cap=Yes.
  2. 2Create a cylinder: draw a Circle (radius 30) centered on the box. Extrude it 80 units, Cap=Yes — it should pass completely through the box.
  3. 3Type BooleanDifference and press Enter.
  4. 4The command asks for the surface to subtract from — click the box. Press Enter.
  5. 5The command asks for the surface to subtract — click the cylinder. Press Enter. A cylindrical hole appears through the box.
💡 Tip: Make sure your cutting tool passes completely through the object being cut. If it only partially intersects, the Boolean may fail or produce unexpected results.
Fig 15. BooleanDifference result — the cylinder subtracted from the base, leaving a clean oval recess

BooleanIntersection — Keeping Overlap Only

BooleanIntersection keeps only the volume where both solids overlap and deletes everything else. Used less frequently but essential for certain design operations.

∩ BooleanIntersection Keep only where two solids overlap ▾
  1. 1Create a box (200 × 200 × 100) and a sphere — type Sphere, click center on top face of box, radius 80.
  2. 2Position them so the sphere partially overlaps the box from above.
  3. 3Type BooleanIntersection and press Enter.
  4. 4Select both objects and press Enter.
  5. 5Only the lens-shaped overlap region remains — the rest of both objects is deleted. View in Shaded mode to see the result clearly.
💡 Tip: BooleanIntersection is great for creating complex organic shapes by intersecting simple primitives — domes, lenses, bevelled corners.
Fig 16. BooleanIntersection result — only the overlapping dome region is kept

Checking for Naked Edges — Critical Before Export

A naked edge is an edge that belongs to only one surface — meaning your solid has a gap or hole in it. This will cause problems in every downstream application — Cura will refuse to slice it, Fusion 360 CAM will misread the geometry, and laser exports may have open contours.

CommandWhat It Does
ShowEdgesHighlights naked edges in magenta — run this before every export
CheckFull geometry analysis — reports naked edges, non-manifold edges, degenerate surfaces
CapCloses planar holes in an open polysurface — fixes common naked edge problems
JoinJoins surfaces sharing edges into a polysurface — run before Cap
MergeAllFacesSimplifies coplanar faces — reduces mesh complexity before export
⚠️ Rule:Always run ShowEdges before exporting any 3D model. If magenta edges appear, fix them before sending to any machine. A model with naked edges will fail in Cura, produce bad toolpaths in Fusion 360, and waste material.
✏ TRY IT  —  Boolean Modelling Project
  1. 1Build a phone stand: start with a box (120 × 80 × 60). Use BooleanDifference to cut a slot (10 × 60 × 40) into the top for the phone to sit in.
  2. 2Cut a cable hole: create a small cylinder (radius 8, height 80) positioned at the base of the slot. Use BooleanDifference to cut it through the back of the stand.
  3. 3Add feet: create four small cylinders (radius 5, height 5) at each bottom corner. Use BooleanUnion to merge them with the stand body.
  4. 4Run ShowEdges — confirm no magenta naked edges appear.
  5. 5Run Check — the result should say "Valid closed polysurface." You are ready to export.
🖨️

Step 1 — Setting Up Your Rhino File for Laser

The Trotec and Ruby use line colour to determine what the laser does. You must set exact RGB colours in Rhino before exporting. This is the most critical step — wrong colours mean wrong operations on the machine.

Colour in RhinoRGB ValueOperation in Ruby
🔴 RedRGB 255, 0, 0Vector Cut — cuts all the way through the material
🔵 BlueRGB 0, 0, 255Vector Engrave — scores the surface without cutting through
⚫ BlackRGB 0, 0, 0Raster Engrave — fills/hatches an area (for images or filled shapes)
⚠️ Exact RGB values:The colour must be exact. Use Object Properties → Display Colour → Custom and type the RGB values manually. Do not use Rhino's layer colour for laser work — set it directly on the object or use dedicated layers named CUT, ENGRAVE, RASTER with the exact colours assigned.

Setting Object Colour in Rhino

Select your cut curves → Properties panel → Display Colour → click the colour swatch → Custom → set R:255, G:0, B:0 → OK. Repeat for engrave lines with blue.

Step 2 — Drawing Rules for Laser Cutting

RuleWhy It Matters
All cut lines must be closed curvesOpen contours will not cut a complete shape — the piece won't fall out
No duplicate linesThe laser will cut the same line twice, burning the material
Minimum line spacing = material thicknessThin bridges between cuts may break or burn through
Draw at 1:1 scale in millimetresWhat you draw is what gets cut — no scaling in Ruby
Keep all geometry in the Top viewportThe laser works in 2D — Z values are ignored
Use Rhino's Join command on cut outlinesJoined curves export as single closed contours

Step 3 — Kerf Compensation

The laser beam has a physical width (the kerf) — typically 0.1–0.2mm on the Trotec Speedy 360 depending on material and lens. This means the actual cut removes a sliver of material, making parts slightly smaller than drawn.

For tight-fitting parts (press-fit joints, finger joints) you need to compensate by offsetting your cut lines outward by half the kerf value. Use Rhino's Offset command — offset your cut curve outward by 0.1mm for a 0.2mm kerf.

💡 Rule of Thumb:For loose/decorative cuts — no compensation needed. For press-fit joints in 3mm acrylic — offset cut lines by 0.1mm outward. For tight finger joints in plywood — test with a sample first, kerf varies by material.

Step 4 — Exporting from Rhino

StepAction
1. Select all geometryCtrl+A to select everything, or select specific layers
2. File → Export SelectedChoose DXF or PDF format
3. DXF settingsExport scheme: R12 Lines & Arcs — keeps colours, simplest format for Ruby
4. PDF settingsSet page size to match your material. Vector output only — no rasterising
5. Check the exportOpen the DXF in a viewer or re-import to Rhino — confirm colours are preserved

Step 5 — Ruby Software Orientation

Fig 17. Ruby (Trotec Laser) — job preparation interface showing design library, bed layout, material selection and job queue

Ruby is Trotec's job management software. It receives your file, maps colours to laser operations, and sends the job to the Speedy 360.

Ruby StepWhat to Do
Import fileFile → Import, or drag your DXF/PDF directly into the Ruby job window
Colour mappingRuby automatically detects your red/blue/black lines and assigns Cut/Engrave/Raster operations
Set materialSelect your material from the database (Acrylic 3mm, Plywood 6mm etc.) — power and speed auto-populate
Job sizeConfirm the job dimensions match your material size and position on the bed
Send to machineClick the play button — the job transfers to the Trotec control panel

Materials on the Trotec Speedy 360

🟣 Acrylic
Cuts cleanly with polished edges. Flame-polished finish. Common thicknesses: 3mm, 5mm. Engrave reveals frosted white mark. No masking needed for cutting.
🪵 Plywood
Cuts well but edges char brown — sand or seal after cutting. Common thicknesses: 3mm, 6mm, 9mm. Engrave removes surface veneer. Check for voids in ply — can cause issues.
✏ LASER PREP CHECKLIST — Before Every Job
  1. 1All cut curves are closed — run SelOpenCrv to find any open curves and fix them.
  2. 2Cut lines are RGB 255,0,0 (exact red). Engrave lines are RGB 0,0,255 (exact blue).
  3. 3No duplicate lines — use SelDup to find and delete duplicates.
  4. 4All geometry is drawn at 1:1 scale in millimetres.
  5. 5File exported as DXF R12 with colours preserved — re-import to verify.
  6. 6In Ruby: colour mapping correct, material selected, job size confirmed.

Two CNC Workflows

WorkflowRhino OutputExport FormatFusion 360 Operation
2D Profile CuttingFlat closed curvesDXF2D Contour, Pocket, Drill
3D Surface Machining3D solid or surfaceSTEP3D Adaptive, Parallel, Scallop

2D Workflow — Profile Cutting in Acrylic & Plywood

The 2D workflow mirrors the laser cutter in concept — you draw flat profiles in Rhino and cut them from sheet material. The key difference is that the CNC router uses a physical spinning bit with a diameter, so you must account for tool radius in your design.

Drawing Rules for CNC 2D Cutting

RuleWhy It Matters
All profiles must be closed curvesOpen contours give Fusion 360 nothing to follow for a complete cut
Minimum inside corner radius = tool radiusA 6mm bit cannot cut a sharp inside corner — minimum radius is 3mm. Use Fillet in Rhino.
Draw at 1:1 scale in millimetresFusion 360 CAM reads actual dimensions from your geometry
Separate layers for cut profiles, pockets, drill pointsMakes toolpath selection in Fusion 360 much easier
Add tabs to cut profilesWithout tabs parts break free mid-cut and become dangerous projectiles
⚠️ Tabs are mandatory:Always include tabs (small bridges of uncut material) when profile cutting on the CNC. Parts that break free from the sheet mid-cut can be thrown by the router bit. Tabs can be added in Fusion 360 CAM — your instructor will demonstrate the minimum tab size and placement for each material.

Exporting 2D from Rhino for CNC

StepAction
1. Select geometrySelect all curves on your cut layer
2. File → Export SelectedChoose DXF format
3. DXF schemeUse R14 Natural or 2007 Natural — preserves layers and line types
4. UnitsConfirm export units are millimetres
5. VerifyImport DXF back into Rhino or open in Fusion 360 — check all curves are present and at correct scale

3D Workflow — Surface Machining

For 3D machining the MultiCam follows the surface of your solid, cutting away material in passes to reveal the 3D form. This requires a solid or surface exported as STEP format — the industry standard for 3D CAM interchange.

Exporting 3D from Rhino for Fusion 360

StepAction
1. Run ShowEdgesConfirm no naked edges on your solid before exporting
2. File → Save As (preferred)Choose 3DM format — Rhino native, best fidelity in Fusion 360
3. Alternative exportFile → Export Selected → STEP (AP214) if 3DM causes issues in Fusion
4. Import to Fusion 360File → Open → upload STEP → confirm geometry imported correctly
5. Set up CAM workspaceSwitch to the Manufacture workspace in Fusion 360

Fusion 360 CAM — Orientation

Fig 18. Fusion 360 Manufacture workspace — CAM toolpaths generated on a 3D surface model imported from Rhino via STEP

Fusion 360's Manufacture workspace is where you define toolpaths — the routes the router bit follows to cut your material. Key concepts for beginners:

ConceptWhat It Means
Setup / StockDefine the block of raw material the part will be cut from — must be larger than your part
Tool selectionChoose the router bit — diameter, flutes, material type affect cut quality
2D ContourCuts around the outside or inside profile of a flat curve
2D PocketClears material inside a closed boundary — for recesses and pockets
DrillSpots or drills holes at point locations
3D AdaptiveEfficient 3D roughing — removes bulk material quickly
3D ParallelFinishing pass — smooth parallel lines across the surface
Inside / OutsideFor contour cuts — inside keeps the part, outside cuts it free
TabsBridges of material that hold the part in place until manual removal
Post processorConverts toolpaths to G-code for the specific MultiCam controller

Materials on the MultiCam

🟣 Acrylic
Requires sharp single-flute bit. Cut slow, high RPM. Chips must clear — use air blast. Tabs essential. Polished cut edges possible with correct feeds.
🪵 Plywood
Most forgiving material for CNC. Two-flute upcut spiral recommended. Check for voids. Down-cut bit gives cleaner top surface. Standard tabs work well.
✏ CNC PREP CHECKLIST — Before Every Job
  1. 1All profiles are closed curves — no open contours.
  2. 2All inside corners have a minimum radius of 3mm (or match your tool radius) — use Fillet.
  3. 3File drawn at 1:1 scale in millimetres.
  4. 4Exported as DXF (2D) or STEP (3D) — verified in Fusion 360.
  5. 5In Fusion 360: correct tool selected, stock defined, inside/outside set correctly, tabs added.
  6. 6Toolpath simulated in Fusion 360 — no collisions, correct cut depth.

The Golden Rule — Watertight Solids Only

The 3D printer pathway has the strictest geometry requirements. Your Rhino model must be a closed watertight polysurface before export. Cura slices the model by intersecting it with horizontal planes — if there are gaps or naked edges, the slicer cannot determine what is inside and outside the model, producing unprintable or incorrect slices.

⚠️ Before every export:Run ShowEdges — zero naked edges required. Then run Check — must say "Valid closed polysurface". If either check fails, do not export. Fix the geometry in Rhino first.

Design Rules for 3D Printing

RuleMinimumWhy
Wall thickness1.2mm minimumThinner walls may not slice or will be too fragile to print
OverhangsMax 45° without supportsBeyond 45° the printer cannot bridge the gap — supports needed
Hole diameter2mm minimumSmaller holes fill with material or don't print accurately
BridgingMax 50mm unsupportedLonger bridges sag — use supports or redesign
Flat baseRecommendedModels print best with a flat face on the build plate
Tolerances for fitsAdd 0.2–0.3mm clearancePrinted parts are slightly larger than modelled — allow for this in joints

Exporting from Rhino for 3D Printing

StepAction
1. Check geometryRun ShowEdges and Check — must be valid closed polysurface
2. Select your solidClick to select the object to export
3. File → Export SelectedChoose STL format
4. STL mesh settingsSet tolerance to 0.01mm. Maximum angle: 20°. This balances file size vs. surface quality.
5. Preview meshRhino shows a mesh preview — check it looks smooth and correct before confirming
6. Alternative: 3MF3MF preserves colour and material data — preferred for multi-material prints
💡 STL Tolerance:A tolerance of 0.01mm gives excellent quality without huge file sizes. Going below 0.005mm creates very large files with diminishing returns. For organic curved surfaces use 0.005mm — for mechanical parts with flat faces 0.01mm is fine.

Cura — Orientation

Fig 19. UltiMaker Cura — STL loaded on the Factor 4 build plate with print settings panel showing layer height, infill and wall settings

Cura is the slicing software that converts your STL into layer-by-layer instructions for the Ultimaker Factor 4. Key settings to understand:

SettingRecommended Starting PointEffect
Layer height0.2mmThinner = smoother surface but longer print. 0.1mm for fine detail, 0.3mm for fast drafts.
Infill density20%How solid the inside is. 20% is good for most parts. 100% for maximum strength.
Infill patternGrid or GyroidGrid is fast, Gyroid gives strength in all directions
Wall line count3 wallsMore walls = stronger and more watertight exterior
SupportsOn for overhangs >45°Temporary support structure removed after printing
Build plate adhesionBrimAdds border around base — prevents warping, especially for ABS
Print temperatureSee material tableSet by material — critical for good layer adhesion

Materials on the Ultimaker Factor 4

🟢 PLA
Easiest to print. 200–215°C nozzle, 60°C bed. Good detail. Brittle under stress. Best for visual models, prototypes, display pieces. Low warping — no enclosure needed.
🟡 ABS
Strong and heat-resistant. 230–245°C nozzle, 100°C bed. High warping — requires enclosed printer and brim. Good for functional mechanical parts. Sand and paint well.
🔵 TPU
Flexible rubber-like material. 220–235°C nozzle, 30–60°C bed. Print slowly. Good for grips, gaskets, phone cases, flexible joints. Difficult to support — design to avoid overhangs.
🟣 Acrylic (resin)
Not used in FDM printing — acrylic is a laser and CNC material. For clear printed parts consider PETG as an alternative on the Factor 4.
✏ 3D PRINT PREP CHECKLIST — Before Every Job
  1. 1Run ShowEdges — zero naked edges. Fix any that appear before continuing.
  2. 2Run Check — result must say "Valid closed polysurface".
  3. 3Minimum wall thickness 1.2mm — check thin areas with OffsetSrf test.
  4. 4All overhangs under 45° — or supports enabled in Cura.
  5. 5Exported as STL at 0.01mm tolerance — mesh preview looks smooth.
  6. 6In Cura: correct material profile selected, layer height set, supports on if needed, print time reviewed.
  7. 7Model oriented in Cura with largest flat face on build plate for best adhesion.
